explanations.explanation: Fury is it, friend. The verse says Jerusalem drank from the hand of the LORD "the cup of His fury." That's a heavy cup, and the next verses show how much of it she took in.

I get why sorrow came to mind, because a cup of sorrow sounds like a sad song on the radio. But the text names a different word: "the cup of His fury." Sorrow is what you feel around it, and fury is what's actually in the cup.

Testing sounds like a reasonable guess, baker, but the verse never uses it. Isaiah says Jerusalem drank "the cup of His fury," and that's the word to hold onto. The text doesn't say why the cup came, so I won't guess either.

I can see why a sip sounds likely, but the text says much more than that. Jerusalem "drained the goblet to the dregs," which means down to the very bottom. A sip leaves some behind, and she left nothing.

That's right. She didn't stop at one sip, because the text says she "drained the goblet to the dregs." That's every last drop, down to the bottom. If I did that with a batch of dough, there'd be nothing left but crumbs and a very guilty mustache.
I wish that were the case, friend, but the verse says the opposite. "Among all the sons she brought up, there is no one to take her hand." She's staggering, and nobody is stepping in to steady her.

That's it. "Your sons have fainted; they lie at the head of every street, like an antelope in a net." They aren't moving around, they're lying down. A net holds an antelope still, and that's the picture Isaiah gives.

explanations.answer: They have run off to hide
explanations.explanation: Hiding would mean going somewhere out of sight, but these sons are in plain view. The verse says they lie at the head of every street. What has happened to them is that they have fainted.
Gathering for battle would mean standing ready, baker, and these sons are anything but ready. The verse says "Your sons have fainted." They lie at the head of every street, like an antelope in a net.
Yes, it says that in the same verse: "They are full of the wrath of the LORD, the rebuke of your God." This is a heavy part, friend. The text doesn't hurry past it, and I won't either.

The text does say it, right there in verse 20: "They are full of the wrath of the LORD, the rebuke of your God." It's a heavy line, and I think it's meant to be felt. The good news is coming, but this is where the passage is at this moment.
That's the turn, friend. The LORD says, "See, I have removed from your hand the cup of staggering." He's the One who defends His people, and He takes the cup out of her hand Himself.
Fill it up again? That's the opposite of what He says. The LORD says, "See, I have removed from your hand the cup of staggering." He doesn't refill it, He takes it away.

Her sons have already fainted at the head of every street, so they're in no shape to take a cup from anybody. The LORD says, "See, I have removed from your hand the cup of staggering." Where the cup goes next comes a verse later, and it isn't her sons.
Never. The LORD says, "From that goblet, the cup of My fury, you will never drink again." That's a promise with no end date and no fine print.
Soon would make it sound like a short break before the next round. But the LORD says, "you will never drink again." There's no waiting period on that.
Always has it backwards, baker. The LORD's words are, "From that goblet, the cup of My fury, you will never drink again." She drained it once, and He says that's the last time.
That's it. The LORD says, "I will place it in the hands of your tormentors." The cup leaves Jerusalem's hand and goes to the ones who tormented her.

The watchmen show up later in this passage, and they're busy shouting for joy, not holding cups. Here the LORD says, "I will place it in the hands of your tormentors." That's where the cup goes.

explanations.answer: Lie down so we can walk over you
explanations.explanation: That's what they said: "Lie down, so we can walk over you." It's a cruel thing to tell anyone. I think we can say once that this one is heavy, and the LORD sees it too.

explanations.answer: Bow down to our gods every day
explanations.explanation: The verse doesn't say anything about gods or bowing every day. What the tormentors told her was, "Lie down, so we can walk over you." It's blunt, and the verse says she made her back like the ground.

explanations.answer: Leave this city and never return
explanations.explanation: They weren't telling her to leave, baker. The tormentors said, "Lie down, so we can walk over you." It's a hard line, and the verse that follows shows how she took it.
Yes. The prophet says, "Put on your garments of splendor, O Jerusalem, holy city!" Strength and splendor, both on together. That's quite a change of outfit from staggering in the street.
Sackcloth and ashes would be a very different wardrobe. The prophet says, "Put on your garments of splendor, O Jerusalem, holy city!" Splendor, baker, not sackcloth.
Widow's clothes aren't anywhere in these verses. The prophet's words are, "Put on your garments of splendor, O Jerusalem, holy city!" Splendor is the order of the day.

There's no price tag on this one. The LORD says, "You were sold for nothing, and without money you will be redeemed." It's the "without money" part that matters here.
Egypt. The LORD says, "At first My people went down to Egypt to live, then Assyria oppressed them without cause." He's looking back over His people's story, one place at a time.
Edom doesn't come up in this verse. The LORD says, "At first My people went down to Egypt to live, then Assyria oppressed them without cause." Egypt is the first stop on that list.
Philistia isn't named here, baker. The verse says, "At first My people went down to Egypt to live," and then it moves on to Assyria, the nation that oppressed them. Egypt is the answer.

Comforted is right. The text says, "the LORD has comforted His people; He has redeemed Jerusalem." Back in chapter 51, the question was who could comfort her, and here is the answer.

Scattered would be bad news, and this verse is about joy. It says, "for the LORD has comforted His people; He has redeemed Jerusalem." The ruins sing because they've been comforted.
Right. The verse says, "all the ends of the earth will see the salvation of our God." It all comes after the LORD has bared His holy arm, and everyone gets to see it, even the far ends of the earth.

explanations.answer: The fall of their own kings
explanations.explanation: No kings are falling in this verse. Isaiah says, "all the ends of the earth will see the salvation of our God." That's what's on display.
Peace is mentioned earlier in the passage, but this verse doesn't say wars end. It says, "all the ends of the earth will see the salvation of our God." That's what everyone gets to see.

explanations.answer: Those who carry the vessels of the LORD
explanations.explanation: Yes. The prophet says, "purify yourselves, you who carry the vessels of the LORD." He's speaking to the ones carrying the LORD's vessels, and he tells them to go out.

explanations.answer: Those who guard the city walls
explanations.explanation: Guards aren't who the prophet calls out here, friend. He says, "purify yourselves, you who carry the vessels of the LORD." The ones carrying the vessels are the ones he tells to purify themselves.

explanations.answer: Those who rebuild the city ruins
explanations.explanation: Rebuilding doesn't come up in this verse. The words are, "purify yourselves, you who carry the vessels of the LORD." That's who gets the call.
It's the other way around, friend. The prophet says, "For you will not leave in a hurry nor flee in haste." So no hurrying and no fleeing.
Right. The text says, "you will not leave in a hurry nor flee in haste." The reason follows right behind it: the LORD goes before them.
Yes. "The LORD goes before you, and the God of Israel is your rear guard." He's out in front and covering the back, so the ones leaving are covered on both sides.
The watchmen are busy shouting for joy a few verses earlier, not guarding the back of this group. The verse says, "the God of Israel is your rear guard." That's the answer.
There's no king's army in these verses, baker. The text says, "the LORD goes before you, and the God of Israel is your rear guard." He's the one covering the back.
